title: Different challenges.
One engineering mindset.
work.lead: My day job runs behind a bank’s walls. These public projects show how I think — with source you can read.
work.note: Public projects, with source and context.

projects.title: Across architectures.
projects.name: Prisma
projects.summary: A binary translator exploring the boundary between machine instructions and portable execution.
projects.problem: How can a binary built for one instruction set run on another and behave exactly the same?
projects.approach: A staged pipeline: decoding, an intermediate representation, optimization, emission and runtime. Each boundary can be inspected and tested on its own.
projects.tradeoff: Translation speed competes with correctness and compatibility. Staging makes validation explicit, at the cost of intermediate structures and more engineering.
projects.outcome: A public translation pipeline, a formal specification area in Lean 4 and an ongoing Rust migration. An evolving research project.
projects.lesson: Ambitious systems are built from small, testable contracts. The most valuable artifact is often the boundary that makes a failure understandable.

projects.title: Carefully connected.
projects.name: Clinic platform
projects.summary: Appointments, inventory and purchasing connected in one product, with a live demo you can click through.
projects.problem: Clinic operations cross several boundaries: scheduling, stock, purchasing and accountability. How do you connect them without losing control?
projects.approach: A public demo and a separate authenticated portal and API. Inventory and purchasing model explicit state changes, permissions and audit records.
projects.tradeoff: Browser-local demo data makes exploring effortless, but cannot offer shared persistence or server authorization. The private API covers that path.
projects.outcome: Documented demo workflows and a local authenticated portal. All demo data is synthetic; production identity and deployment are separate work.
projects.lesson: A convincing product shows its operating limits. Being clear about what is simulated lets a reviewer judge the architecture honestly.

projects.title: Knowledge that ships.
projects.name: DevOps learning lab
projects.summary: One application. An entire delivery lifecycle. A four-day course that teaches systems thinking by doing.
projects.problem: Teaching tools in isolation hides how software actually becomes an operated service.
projects.approach: One application travels from source control through containers, delivery automation, orchestration, monitoring and security, with bilingual guides and debugging exercises.
projects.tradeoff: A coherent learning path favors a small, reproducible environment over the full complexity of a production platform. Intentional failures make the limits teachable.
projects.outcome: A four-day curriculum with application examples, deployment manifests, instructor material and troubleshooting exercises.
projects.lesson: Technical leadership scales through artifacts people can use on their own: runnable examples, decision guides and clear recovery paths.

title: The interesting part?
What happens when it breaks.
lab.lead: Fallback and rollback planning is part of my daily work on Tier-0 payments. Here is the idea in miniature: take down the primary and watch the traffic move.
lab.svgDesc: A client connects to a router, which uses the primary service or a standby service. Both lead to a response.
lab.noscript: The diagram shows normal operation. JavaScript enables the failure and recovery scenarios.
lab.disclaimer: Illustrative simulation: latencies are fixed scenario values, not measurements from a live service. Real failover also needs data consistency, capacity and health-check policies.

healthy.title: Primary route active
healthy.description: The router sends every request to the primary service. The standby stays warm, ready for a failover.
healthy.tradeoff: Redundancy buys recovery options, at the cost of running an additional service.

failed.title: Standby route active
failed.description: The primary is down. The router detects it and redirects new requests to the standby; the extra hop raises latency, but nothing is dropped.
failed.tradeoff: Availability is preserved at the cost of an extra hop. Real systems must also validate standby capacity and data consistency.

recovered.title: Primary restored after health checks
recovered.description: Recovery checks have passed. New requests return to the primary while the standby stays ready.
recovered.tradeoff: Returning traffic only after recovery checks avoids flapping. Real systems need a stabilization window and explicit failback criteria.

title: Deep in the details.
Connected to the whole.
paragraphs: I’m Daniel, a Senior Full-Stack Engineer based in Toluca, México.

I have built enterprise software for more than seven years, most of them where software meets money: real-time payments, the platforms that run them and the teams that keep them healthy. I’m drawn to the moment a hard technical problem becomes something people can understand, use and trust.
